mcqs.question: What is the correct way to describe CSP's role relative to output encoding?
options: CSP replaces output encoding, since the browser blocks injected script anyway
CSP validates untrusted input before it reaches the rendering layer
CSP and output encoding are alternatives; you pick whichever fits the stack
Encoding reduces the chance of an injection; CSP reduces what an injection can do
mcqs.explanation: They act at different points — encoding prevents the untrusted string being parsed as markup, while CSP is the browser-side control that limits execution if something slipped through. Treating CSP as a replacement is the classic mistake, since injections that deface a page or plant a fake login form need no script execution at all.

mcqs.question: Your policy is `default-src 'self'` and nothing else. Which of these is still unrestricted?
options: Which hosts `fetch` and WebSocket connections may reach
Who is allowed to embed your page in an iframe
Which hosts scripts may be loaded from
Which hosts images may be loaded from
mcqs.explanation: `frame-ancestors` does not fall back to `default-src` and must be set explicitly, alongside `base-uri` and `form-action` — so framing is wide open under this policy. Script, connect and image sources do inherit the `default-src` value, which is exactly why that fallback is a useful floor but not a complete policy.

mcqs.question: A statically exported site is served from a CDN as one cached HTML artifact. Why are hashes preferable to nonces here?
options: A nonce must be fresh per response, which cached HTML cannot provide, whereas a hash pins fixed inline content at build time
Hashes are cryptographically stronger than nonces
Nonces only work with `'strict-dynamic'`, which CDNs strip
CDNs are not permitted to serve responses carrying a CSP header
mcqs.explanation: The security of a nonce depends on being unpredictable and different on every response, and a single cached artifact would serve the same value to everyone — which is equivalent to no nonce. A hash pins the exact inline content instead, needs no per-response randomness, and is computed during the build.

mcqs.question: Your CSP report endpoint is flooded with violations for inline scripts with no line number or recognisable source. What is the most likely explanation?
options: An ongoing XSS campaign that should be escalated immediately
The nonce is being cached and reused across responses
Browser extensions injecting content into the page
The policy is malformed, so the browser reports every load
mcqs.explanation: Extension-injected content is the single largest source of report noise in real deployments, which is why triage means filtering it out rather than allowlisting the sources it names. A genuine attack is possible but would not be the base rate, and a malformed directive is ignored by browsers rather than causing blanket reporting.

mcqs.question: Why is `script-src 'self' https://cdn.popular-vendor.com` often trivially bypassable?
options: Because `'self'` implicitly allows any subdomain of your own domain
Because the browser ignores host allowlists when more than one host is named
Because popular CDNs may host JSONP endpoints or old library builds that execute attacker-chosen code, so allowlisting the host allowlists arbitrary script
Because host allowlists are only advisory and are not enforced by browsers
mcqs.explanation: The policy authorises an origin, not particular files, so any endpoint on that origin capable of running caller-supplied code effectively grants arbitrary execution — this is why large-scale analyses found most domain-allowlist policies bypassable. Nonce-based policies avoid it by authorising specific script elements rather than whole hosts.

mcqs.question: A release is blocked by CSP because a page has an inline bootstrap script. What is the right fix?
options: Add the per-response nonce to that script tag
Add `'unsafe-inline'` to `script-src` and open a ticket to remove it later
Move the policy from the header into a `<meta>` tag, which is less strict
Switch `script-src` to `default-src` so the inline script inherits a looser rule
mcqs.explanation: Adding the nonce authorises exactly that block while leaving everything else blocked, and it is usually a smaller change than it appears. `'unsafe-inline'` permits any inline script — precisely the capability an XSS payload needs — so it removes the policy's main purpose, and the ticket to remove it reliably outlives the person who filed it.
